Mecka AI raised $60 million in Series B funding from Sequoia, Nvidia, and Microsoft's M12 to pay everyday people to record household tasks for humanoid robot training.

The Poison:
Heavy reliance on low-cost gig labor to capture domestic tasks risks high noise ratios, sensor drift, and repetitive-data saturation.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
This venture links Physical (WHERE) sensor telemetry with Logical (HOW) robotics training, transferring the Scale AI data brokerage blueprint to kinematics.

Social Physics Analysis:
The company applies standard venture scaling to robotics data bottlenecks. By turning mundane domestic labor into tokenized training feeds, it builds value across software and hardware ecosystems.

The Trajectory: The Path of Stasis in Grace.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Good. Capital reliably accelerates robotics infrastructure.

The Unavoidable Truth: Humanoid robots cannot generalize in physical spaces without massive volumes of real-world motion data.
The Unavoidable Lie: Simple smartphone videos will instantly solve fine-motor manipulation for robots.

Alethekanon:
The funding validates data brokerage as the bottleneck for robotics, though data cleanliness remains the central technical hurdle.

Awwthekanon:
It is fascinating to see ordinary human chores like making coffee become valuable lessons for teaching the machines of tomorrow.

Scale AI got rich selling text data to chatbots, and now Mecka is raising big cash to pay people to wear sensors while making toast.

Posted:

Mecka AI, a startup that collects and analyzes human motion data to train humanoid robots and other kinds of robots, announced it has raised a $60 million Series B round led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Microsoft’s venture fund M12, and others. TechCrunch had previously reported that the startup was nearing a new funding round at a $500 million valuation.

Founded in 2024, the startup intends to do for robotics what Scale AI, Mercor, Surge, and other data-labeling companies have done for LLMs. Those companies supply the human-generated data these systems learn from. Mecka pays people to record themselves doing everyday tasks, like making coffee or fixing cars, while wearing body sensors and using smartphones.

Other startups that collect real-world data for robot training include XDOF, which was in talks to raise a Series B round at a $1.2 billion valuation according to TechCrunch’s previous reporting. Human-data platforms that began with LLMs are also expanding into robotics, such as Scale AI and Micro1.
